points: An interface (or API) describes what operations are available, not how they are carried out.
The interface specifies *what* you want to do; the data structure specifies *how* it is done.
The data structure provides the concrete representation and tells you how to store the data.
Storing data alone is trivial; the interesting part is defining operations that act on that data.
An interface lists the supported operations and their intended behavior.
The data structure supplies the algorithms that implement those operations.
The course will concentrate on two primary interfaces and their special cases, emphasizing the separation of what to do from how to do it.
A single problem can be solved by many different data structures, each offering different performance trade‑offs for the supported operations.
We choose a data structure based on which operations need to be fast for our particular use case, while keeping the same abstract interface.
The two primary abstract data types we will study are the set and the sequence.
In Python a list can be used to store a sequence, preserving the order of elements (first, second, …, last).
The lecture will concentrate on the sequence abstract data type for the next several lectures, postponing the set interface until later.
Intro to Algorithms is taught by Jason Ku together with Eric Domen and Justin Solomon.
Jason will teach the first lecture; the next two lectures will be taught by the other instructors.
Goal: teach you to solve computational problems.
The course involves considerably more writing than typical coding courses.
Goal: prove solutions correct, show they are better, and convey this to people, not just computers.
A computational problem consists of a set of possible inputs to an algorithm.
Along with a space of possible outputs, which may be larger than the input set.
Formally, a problem is a binary relation between inputs and outputs, specifying which outputs are correct for each input.
An input may correspond to multiple possible outputs; e.g., an index of value 5 in an array could be any of several positions.
The relation can be visualized as a graph where edges connect inputs to their admissible outputs.
Welcome to the first class of 6.001 (and 6.600) this semester.
The lecture will later cover basic administrative info and then discuss what computation is at a high level.
We'll start with Python basics, including the mathematical operations you can perform in Python.
The lecture will also cover Python types, which are the kinds of data values you can work with.
All slides and code examples will be uploaded before class; students are encouraged to download them in advance.
Class exercises are embedded in the slides; taking notes on the code is recommended for future reference.
Practice is essential: like math or reading, the more you code, the better you become.
Download the code before the lecture and follow along as you type the examples yourself.
If you make a mistake, just restart the computer – you won’t break it by typing commands in Anaconda.
The course aims for three outcomes: grasping programming concepts, building programming skills, and learning problem‑solving through p‑sets.
The course content is divided into three main sections.
The first section focuses on learning how to program, including deciding which objects to create.
